Name: aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]
Structural Path: key -> aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0] -> round-key generation -> AddRoundKey -> AES state -> text_out
Attack Scenarios: RTL connectivity realizes this dependence as `aes_cipher_top.key -> aes_cipher_top.u0.key -> aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]`. The key-expansion register `aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]` executes its load arm and captures `key[127:96]` without transformation. A scan read or internal probe of `aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]` during or after this load obtains that 32-bit portion of the primary key directly. One quarter of the 128-bit AES key is disclosed from a single observation, and the four word registers together reveal the complete key.

RTL connectivity realizes this dependence as `aes_cipher_top.key -> aes_cipher_top.u0.key -> aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]`. On later rising edges with `kld = 0`, the key schedule updates its word registers using XORs of prior words, `subword`, and `rcon`. `aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]` then holds a deterministic expanded-key word and drives the corresponding `wo_0` round-key output. Observing `aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]` over one or more expansion cycles yields round-key material; a complete round key can be inverted through the AES-128 key schedule. The original key can be reconstructed from the collected expanded words even after the direct key-load window has passed.

Because word 0 preserves master-key dependence along the cipher datapath, the documented behavior makes `aes_cipher_top.u0.w[0]` relevant to compromise of `key`.
